title: Understanding React's types
summary: Matt Pocock live-streams an unplanned exploration of React's TypeScript type definitions with his chat. Starting from the observation that @types/react is full of overlapping types (ReactNode, ReactElement, JSX.Element, React.FC, PropsWithChildren, ComponentProps), he sets out to map how they relate to each other, installing @types/react in a scratch project, reading the actual .d.ts unions, and brute-force testing assignability between types. The core discovery of the stream is an asymmetry: ReactNode is everything you can render inside a component, but you can only return ReactElement (or JSX.Element, ReactPortal, or null) from a component - strings, numbers, booleans, and undefined render fine as children yet are rejected as return values, because the JSX legality rules are implemented by TypeScript's global JSX namespace, not by React. He verifies behavior in a CodeSandbox on React 18, draws a Venn diagram of the finding in tldraw, and tweets it.
what_you_learn: You learn how to read a large third-party .d.ts file and reverse-engineer a type taxonomy by probing assignability instead of trusting names - a skill that transfers directly to understanding any unfamiliar type-driven library. You also get the precise mental model of ReactNode vs ReactElement vs JSX.Element that most React developers guess at wrong.

skills.name: TypeScript Type System
skills.description: Using ComponentProps, ComponentPropsWithoutRef, and PropsWithChildren to wrap DOM elements and inherit their props.

learnings.title: React does not ship its own types - you install @types/react
learnings.detail: Matt starts with pnpm add react plus pnpm add -D @types/react. The type definitions are maintained separately from the React team itself, which is part of why the integration between React and TypeScript has rough edges - he mentions discussing exactly this with Dan Abramov on Twitter.

learnings.title: ReactNode is everything React can render
learnings.detail: ReactNode is a big union: ReactElement, string, number, ReactFragment, ReactPortal, boolean, null, and undefined. If a value can appear between JSX tags, it is a ReactNode. Matt uses it as the type for a children prop so callers can pass divs, text, or fragments.

learnings.title: React.FC returns ReactElement or null and nothing else
learnings.detail: React.FC (functional component) types the return as ReactElement | null, which is why you cannot return a bare string from an FC-annotated component even though strings render fine as children. Matt also notes compound components are a mess with React.FC, and that VoidFunctionComponent (VFC) is deprecated.

learnings.title: ComponentProps is the idiomatic way to wrap a DOM element
learnings.detail: To build a component that wraps a div and inherits all its HTML attributes, type the props as ComponentProps<'div'> and spread them into the div. It is assignable only for matching elements - passing 'span' fails because the prop sets differ - and you can override individual props like className for Tailwind styling.

learnings.title: JSX.Element is a shim over ReactElement owned by TypeScript
learnings.detail: JSX.Element extends React.ReactElement, and its definition lives in the global JSX namespace that comes from React's types but is interpreted by TypeScript. The inferred return type of any component you write is JSX.Element - a 'magic' type that is not string, number, or boolean, just the value TypeScript accepts as a component return.

learnings.title: The core asymmetry: renderable inside is not returnable
learnings.detail: The stream's central finding: ReactNode is what you can render inside a component, but a component may only return ReactElement, JSX.Element, ReactPortal, or null. Strings, numbers, booleans, and undefined all render as children but are compile errors as return values - verified live in a CodeSandbox on React 18 where returning undefined and strings actually works at runtime.

learnings.title: React decides nothing about JSX legality - TypeScript does
learnings.detail: Why the asymmetry exists: React does not define what legal JSX is; TypeScript's JSX namespace does, via JSX.Element. Matt tells the story of trying at Vercel (before NextConf) to override JSX.Element so React Server Components' async components returning JSX could be typed - a Promise could not be passed to a slot expecting a component, and there was no clean way to override it precisely because that logic lives in TypeScript, not React.

learnings.title: Brute-force assignability checks map a type system faster than docs
learnings.detail: Matt empirically probes the relationships: JSX.Element is assignable to ReactElement (so JSX.Element is contained in it), ReactPortal is assignable to ReactElement, but ReactFragment is not, and string, number, boolean, null, and undefined are not valid JSX elements. Arrays of ReactNode are technically ReactFragment. This testing-in-the-editor approach is how you truly learn a type library.

learnings.title: The practical rules to write down
learnings.detail: Concrete takeaways: use ReactNode for anything rendered as children; annotate component return types as ReactElement (optionally | null since null cannot be returned alone under JSX.Element); use ComponentProps<'div'> style helpers when wrapping elements; you cannot restrict what props parents pass to your children; and do not call components manually - let React handle reconciliation.

learnings.title: The Venn diagram takeaway that went to Twitter
learnings.detail: Matt condenses the finding into one tweet: ReactNode is the type you can render inside a component; ReactElement or null is what you can return from a component - 'why the two are different I have no clue.' He builds a green/red Venn diagram in tldraw showing the renderable set containing the returnable set.

key_points: ReactNode is what you can render inside a component; ReactElement or null is what you can return.
JSX.Element is defined by TypeScript's JSX namespace, not by React.
Strings, numbers, booleans, and undefined render fine as children but fail as component return types.
ComponentProps<'div'> is the cleanest way to inherit a DOM element's props when wrapping it.
ReactChild and VFC are deprecated - read .d.ts files before trusting old tutorials.
Never call components manually; let React run reconciliation.
When a type system confuses you, probe assignability in the editor instead of reading docs.
